title: How surprising is this coin?
prompts: Keep p(heads) = 0.5, press Start, and watch the two bars (0 = tails, 1 = heads) level out. Each fair flip carries exactly 1 bit: −log₂(½).
Pause after a few dozen flips. Streaks and lopsided bars are normal; the coin never 'owes' you tails. Only the long-run fraction settles.
Set p(heads) = 0.9. Heads now carries −log₂ 0.9 ≈ 0.15 bits and tails −log₂ 0.1 ≈ 3.32 bits. Which bar delivers the rare, loud news?
Still at 0.9: the average surprise is 0.9 × 0.15 + 0.1 × 3.32 ≈ 0.47 bits per flip. Predict whether 0.99 gives more or less, then check: about 0.08 bits.
Slide p from 0 to 1 and track the binary entropy H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p): 0 bits at the ends, a 1-bit peak at 0.5, symmetric around it.
Raise flips per tick to 200. The yellow expected line is the model; the bars are the evidence. Entropy is a property of the model, not of any single run.
